title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 2 — Interpretation clause

content.overview: Section 2 supplies the core vocabulary of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Clauses (a) to (j) define proposal, promise, promisor and promisee, consideration, agreement, reciprocal promises, void agreement, contract, voidable contract and a contract that becomes void. These definitions form the conceptual chain used throughout the Act.

sections.heading: Proposal — section 2(a)
sections.body: A person makes a proposal when they signify to another their willingness to do or abstain from doing something with a view to obtaining that person's assent. The definition focuses on communicated willingness directed toward obtaining assent. It is the statutory starting point for offer-and-acceptance analysis.

sections.heading: Promise — section 2(b)
sections.body: When the person to whom a proposal is made signifies assent, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise. Thus proposal precedes acceptance, and acceptance transforms the proposal into a promise.

sections.heading: Promisor and promisee — section 2(c)
sections.body: The maker of a proposal is called the promisor and the person accepting it is called the promisee. The labels identify the parties to the promise and support later provisions dealing with performance and reciprocal obligations.

sections.heading: Consideration — section 2(d)
sections.body: Consideration is an act, abstinence or promise done, abstained from or promised at the desire of the promisor by the promisee or another person. The statutory definition expressly permits consideration to move from the promisee or any other person, while requiring that it be at the promisor's desire.

sections.heading: Agreement — section 2(e)
sections.body: Every promise and every set of promises forming the consideration for each other is an agreement. The definition links promise and consideration and provides the statutory bridge between individual promises and bilateral contractual arrangements.

sections.heading: Reciprocal promises — section 2(f)
sections.body: Promises which form the consideration or part of the consideration for each other are reciprocal promises. The concept becomes important in the later provisions governing performance of reciprocal promises.

sections.heading: Void agreement — section 2(g)
sections.body: An agreement not enforceable by law is void. The definition describes the legal consequence; the reason for non-enforceability must be found in the applicable substantive provision, such as a provision expressly declaring a particular agreement void.

sections.heading: Contract — section 2(h)
sections.body: An agreement enforceable by law is a contract. This is the central statutory definition. Section 10 supplies important conditions for when agreements are contracts, so section 2(h) should not be read in isolation.

sections.heading: Voidable contract — section 2(i)
sections.body: A contract is voidable when it is enforceable by law at the option of one or more of the parties to it, but not at the option of the other or others. The definition captures a contract whose enforceability depends on the protected party's election, subject to the relevant substantive provisions.

sections.heading: Contract becomes void — section 2(j)
sections.body: A contract that ceases to be enforceable by law becomes void when, and to the extent, its enforceability is lost. This definition is distinct from an agreement that was void from the beginning and must be applied with the substantive rule governing the event that destroys enforceability.

sections.heading: The statutory chain
sections.body: The definitions form a sequence: proposal → acceptance → promise; promises may form an agreement; an agreement that is enforceable by law is a contract; an agreement that is not enforceable is void; and a contract that later ceases to be enforceable becomes void. Consideration and reciprocal promises operate within this framework.

definitions.meaning: Signified willingness to do or abstain from doing something, made with a view to obtaining the other person's assent.
A proposal that has been accepted.
The person who makes the proposal.
The person who accepts the proposal.
An act, abstinence or promise done, abstained from or promised at the promisor's desire by the promisee or any other person.
Every promise and every set of promises forming consideration for each other.
Promises that form the consideration or part of the consideration for each other.
An agreement not enforceable by law.
A contract enforceable by law at the option of one or more parties, but not at the option of the other party or parties.
A contract that ceases to be enforceable by law becomes void.

statutoryFramework: The definitions operate with the substantive provisions that determine formation, validity, performance, discharge and remedies.
essentialIngredients: Proposal requires signified willingness directed toward obtaining assent.
Acceptance converts a proposal into a promise.
Promisor and promisee identify the parties to the promise.
Consideration must be at the desire of the promisor and may move from the promisee or another person.
Agreement consists of promise or promises forming consideration for each other.
Reciprocal promises are promises that provide consideration or part of consideration for each other.
Void agreement means non-enforceability by law.
Contract means an agreement enforceable by law.
Voidable contract is enforceable at the protected party's option.
A contract that ceases to be enforceable becomes void.
content.detailedExplanation: Section 2 is not merely a dictionary. Its definitions create the conceptual architecture of the Act. Proposal and acceptance describe the formation sequence. Promise identifies the legal commitment resulting from acceptance. Consideration explains the statutory basis for exchange within an agreement. Agreement and contract must be kept distinct: every contract is an agreement, but an agreement is a contract only when it is enforceable by law. The distinction between void and voidable arrangements is equally important. A void agreement lacks enforceability, whereas a voidable contract remains enforceable unless and until the party entitled to avoid it exercises the relevant option. Section 2(j) addresses a different situation: a contract that was enforceable but later ceases to be enforceable. The precise reason for that loss must be traced to the operative substantive provision.

examples.title: Proposal and promise
examples.body: A tells B, 'I will sell you my laptop for ₹40,000,' intending to obtain B's assent. B communicates acceptance. A's proposal has become a promise.

examples.title: Consideration at promisor's desire
examples.body: A asks B to perform a specified service and promises payment. B performs the service at A's request. The service can constitute consideration because it was undertaken at A's desire.

examples.title: Agreement and contract
examples.body: Two parties make an agreement, but a separate statutory rule makes that type of agreement unenforceable. It may be an agreement within section 2(e) but not a contract under section 2(h).

examples.title: Voidable contract
examples.body: A contract is entered into in circumstances giving one party a statutory option to avoid it. Until the protected party exercises the applicable right and subject to the governing provision, the arrangement is not simply treated as a void agreement from the outset.

examples.title: Contract becoming void
examples.body: A contract that was initially enforceable may later cease to be enforceable because of an event or statutory rule. Section 2(j) describes the resulting status; the operative provision determines why enforceability ceased.

hypotheticals.question: A sends a statement to B without intending to obtain B's assent. Is every such statement a proposal?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 2(a) requires willingness to do or abstain from doing something with a view to obtaining the other person's assent. Identify that intention and the communicated willingness before treating the statement as a proposal.

hypotheticals.question: A promises to pay B for an act B performs at A's request. Can the act be consideration?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 2(d) expressly focuses on an act, abstinence or promise at the desire of the promisor and permits the consideration to move from the promisee or another person. The factual inquiry is therefore whether the act was undertaken at A's desire.

hypotheticals.question: Is every agreement a contract?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 2(e) defines agreement, while section 2(h) requires enforceability by law before an agreement is a contract. Section 10 and other provisions supply the substantive conditions for enforceability.

hypotheticals.question: What is the difference between a void agreement and a voidable contract?
hypotheticals.analysis: A void agreement is not enforceable by law under section 2(g). A voidable contract remains enforceable at the option of the party or parties given that option under section 2(i), subject to the relevant substantive provision.

hypotheticals.question: A contract later loses enforceability. Should it be described as void from inception?
hypotheticals.analysis: Not automatically. Section 2(j) addresses a contract that ceases to be enforceable. The analysis must identify the event or statutory provision causing the later loss of enforceability rather than retroactively assuming initial invalidity.

distinctions.title: Proposal vs promise
distinctions.point: A proposal is willingness directed toward obtaining assent; a promise is a proposal after acceptance.

distinctions.title: Agreement vs contract
distinctions.point: An agreement is defined in section 2(e); a contract is an agreement enforceable by law under section 2(h).

distinctions.title: Void vs voidable
distinctions.point: A void agreement is not enforceable by law; a voidable contract remains enforceable at the option of the party entitled to avoid it.

distinctions.title: Void agreement vs contract becoming void
distinctions.point: The former is defined by present non-enforceability of an agreement; section 2(j) concerns a contract that later ceases to be enforceable.

distinctions.title: Consideration vs reciprocal promises
distinctions.point: Consideration is defined by section 2(d); reciprocal promises are promises forming consideration or part of consideration for each other under section 2(f).

content.problemApplication: When analysing a contract problem, identify the relevant section 2 concept before applying the substantive rule. Ask in sequence: Was there a proposal? Was it accepted, producing a promise? What consideration is alleged and at whose desire? Do the promises form an agreement? Is the agreement enforceable by law? If enforceability depends on one party's option, identify the applicable voidable-contract rule. If a previously enforceable contract later ceases to be enforceable, identify the event and substantive provision producing that result. Do not use the definitions as substitutes for the operative provisions that determine legal consequences.
content.currentLaw: Section 2 remains the interpretation clause of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Its definitions must be read contextually, as the section itself qualifies them by the phrase 'unless a contrary intention appears from the context'. Later amendments, special statutes and judicial interpretation may affect how a defined term operates in a particular provision; the definition should therefore be applied together with the operative statutory rule.
keyTakeaways: Section 2 provides the core vocabulary of Indian contract law.
Proposal plus acceptance produces a promise.
Consideration under section 2(d) is tied to the desire of the promisor and may move from the promisee or another person.
An agreement is not necessarily a contract; enforceability by law is required.
Void, voidable and later-void arrangements are distinct legal categories.
